entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The one thing that finally decides a choice or a result when the other things are about equal.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and reviews: *the deciding factor in + decision*, *the deciding factor for + person*, *the deciding factor was …*. It almost always takes *the*, because there is only one. The same adjective appears in *the deciding vote* and *the deciding game*.
entries.pattern: the deciding factor (in + decision / for + someone)
examples: Both apartments were nice, but the shorter commute was **the deciding factor**.
For most buyers, battery life is **the deciding factor** when they choose a phone.
The wind turned out to be **the deciding factor** in the final round of the golf tournament.

drill.sentence: Honestly, the free parking was {{the deciding factor}} when we picked this gym over the one downtown.
drill.hint: the thing that finally made up our minds (not *the clincher* or *the tiebreaker*)

entries.related: *the clincher* — informal, the fact that settles it; *a tiebreaker* — decides between equal options, especially in games; *a contributing factor* — one of several causes.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To complete your tax return and send it to the government, in the US to the IRS and usually to your state.
entries.usage: The everyday American phrase; the deadline is usually April 15, so people talk about it every spring. Typical forms are *file my taxes (online)*, *file a tax return* and *file for an extension*. *Do your taxes* is the casual version, and *pay your taxes* is about the money, not the forms.
entries.pattern: file your taxes (online / by April 15) / file a tax return
examples: I always wait until the last week to **file my taxes**, and I always regret it.
Most people **file their taxes** online now, and refunds usually arrive within a few weeks.
My parents pay an accountant to **file their taxes** because they own a small farm.

drill.sentence: The deadline to {{file your taxes}} is April fifteenth, unless you ask for an extension.
drill.hint: send in your tax return (verb: not *do*, *pay* or *submit*)

mistake.wrong: I still have to make my taxes this weekend.
mistake.right: I still have to file my taxes this weekend.
mistake.why: English uses *file* (official) or *do* (casual) with *taxes*; German *die Steuer machen* leads learners to say *make*.

entries.related: *do your taxes* — casual; *a tax return* — the form itself; *get a refund* — receive money back from the government.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: So slow that it becomes frustrating or annoying to wait or to watch.
entries.usage: Common in complaints about internet speed, traffic, service, progress and the pace of movies or books: *painfully slow Wi-Fi*, *progress has been painfully slow*. *Painfully* adds emotion, not physical pain. The adverb also pairs with *obvious* and *aware*: *painfully obvious*, *painfully aware*.
entries.pattern: painfully slow + noun / be painfully slow
examples: The line at the post office was **painfully slow**; only one clerk was working.
Repairs on the bridge have been **painfully slow**, and traffic is still a mess.
The first half of the movie is **painfully slow**, but the ending is worth the wait.

drill.sentence: The hotel Wi-Fi was so {{painfully slow}} that I couldn't even open my email.
drill.hint: frustratingly sluggish (the adverb suggests hurting)

entries.related: *agonizingly slow* — even stronger; *sluggish* — slow and without energy; *at a snail's pace* — informal, very slowly.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A moment or event that shows what someone or something really is, or that shapes what they become.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, speeches, sports and biographies: *a defining moment in / of / for + someone's life / career*. It sounds serious and a little dramatic, so it suits big events, not small daily choices. *A turning point* is similar but stresses a change of direction rather than identity.
entries.pattern: a defining moment in / of / for + someone / something
examples: Winning that state championship was **a defining moment** in her career.
For my dad, losing his job at fifty was **a defining moment**; he went back to school and became a nurse.
The moon landing was **a defining moment** for a whole generation of Americans.

drill.sentence: Saying yes to that year abroad was {{a defining moment}} in my life; I'd be a different person without it.
drill.hint: an event that shaped who I am (not *a turning point*)

entries.related: *a turning point* — the moment things change direction; *a watershed moment* — a historic change, formal; *a milestone* — an important stage reached.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To ask a company, store or restaurant to supply goods or food, usually by phone, online or at a counter.
entries.usage: Common in business, shopping and customer service: *place an order for + goods*, *place an order with + company*, *place an order online*. It is a little more formal than the verb *order*; in a restaurant the server simply asks *Are you ready to order?* *Put in an order* is a casual variant.
entries.pattern: place an order (for + goods / with + company / online)
examples: I **placed an order** for new running shoes on Monday, and they arrived the next day.
To **place an order**, call our office or use the form on our website.
The airline has **placed an order** for forty new jets.

drill.sentence: The bakery asks customers to {{place an order}} at least two days ahead for birthday cakes.
drill.hint: ask the store to make or supply something (verb + noun; not *put in*)

mistake.wrong: I gave an order for two new chairs last week.
mistake.right: I placed an order for two new chairs last week.
mistake.why: *Give an order* means to command someone; when you buy something, you *place* an order (German *eine Bestellung aufgeben*).

entries.related: *order* — the plain verb; *put in an order* — informal; *cancel an order* — the opposite; *give an order* — command someone.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A person, company or country that has a lot of power and influence in a particular field or market.
entries.usage: Common in business and news: *a major player in + industry / market*, *become a major player*. It is neutral to positive and usually describes organizations or powerful people, not ordinary individuals. *A key player* is similar; *a big player* is more informal.
entries.pattern: a major player in + industry / market
examples: In just five years, the startup has become **a major player** in electric bikes.
Brazil is **a major player** in the global coffee market.
After the merger, the combined bank became **a major player** in the Midwest.

drill.sentence: With stores in every state, the company is now {{a major player}} in the pet food business.
drill.hint: an important, powerful company (adjective + noun; not *key* or *big*)

entries.related: *a key player* — important to a group or result; *a heavyweight* — informal, very powerful; *a newcomer* — new in a field.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely important, often because safety, health or success depends on it.
entries.usage: Common in formal speech, health advice, safety information and business: *it's vitally important to + verb / that …*, *vitally important for / to + noun*. It is stronger and a little more formal than *very important*; *crucial* and *vital* alone are close. In casual talk it can sound dramatic.
entries.pattern: it's vitally important to + verb / that … / vitally important for + noun
examples: It's **vitally important** to drink enough water when you hike in the desert.
Early diagnosis is **vitally important** for children with hearing problems.
Volunteers are **vitally important** to the food bank; it couldn't run without them.

drill.sentence: When you're caring for a newborn, it's {{vitally important}} that you wash your hands often.
drill.hint: needed above almost everything else, for safety (the adverb is not *extremely*, *really* or *critically*)

entries.related: *crucial / vital* — one-word forms; *critically important* — similar, formal; *of the utmost importance* — very formal.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Not at all; definitely not. It makes a negative statement stronger.
entries.usage: Common in writing and careful speech: *It's by no means perfect*, *by no means the only option*. At the start of a sentence it needs inversion, as in a question: *By no means is this easy.* Do not confuse it with *by all means*, which means *of course, please do*.
entries.pattern: be by no means + adjective / noun / By no means + auxiliary + subject
examples: The hotel was **by no means** cheap, but the view made it worth it.
Winning the first game is **by no means** a guarantee that we'll make the playoffs.
**By no means** should you sign the lease before you've seen the apartment.

drill.sentence: This recipe is {{by no means}} difficult; even my twelve-year-old can make it.
drill.hint: definitely not (three words; not *not at all* or *in no way*)

mistake.wrong: Can I borrow your pen? — By no means, go ahead.
mistake.right: Can I borrow your pen? — By all means, go ahead.
mistake.why: *By all means* means *of course*; *by no means* means *definitely not*.

entries.related: *not at all* — plainer; *far from* — *far from perfect*, also common; *by all means* — the opposite: of course, go ahead.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To find and hire someone for a job that is open.
entries.usage: Common in hiring, HR and business news: *fill a position / role / vacancy*, often in the passive: *The position has been filled.* The subject is the employer; the person hired *takes* or *gets* the job. *Fill in for someone* is different: it means to replace someone for a short time.
entries.pattern: fill a position / the position has been filled
examples: We're hoping to **fill the position** by the end of the month.
Rural hospitals often struggle to **fill nursing positions**.
The youth soccer league still hasn't **filled the position** of head referee.

drill.sentence: The school has been trying for months to {{fill the position}} of music teacher.
drill.hint: hire someone for the open job (the noun is not *role* or *vacancy*)

entries.related: *fill a vacancy* — more formal, more British; *hire* — the plain verb; *fill in for someone* — replace someone for a short time.

entries.label: noun + noun
entries.meaning: A question you ask after hearing an answer, to get more detail or to make it clearer.
entries.usage: Common in interviews, press conferences, meetings and classes: *ask a follow-up question*, *Can I ask a quick follow-up?* Before a noun it has a hyphen (*a follow-up question / email*); the verb has none (*follow up on something*).
entries.pattern: ask (someone) a follow-up question (about + topic)
examples: The reporter asked **a follow-up question**, and the CEO suddenly looked uncomfortable.
After the doctor explained my test results, I had **a follow-up question** about side effects.
Sorry, just **a quick follow-up question**: does the price include tax?

drill.sentence: The interviewer liked my answer and asked {{a follow-up question}} about how I handle conflict.
drill.hint: something more to ask, based on my answer (hyphenated adjective + noun; not *another*)

entries.related: *follow up on* — the phrasal verb: check on or continue something; *a clarifying question* — asks what something means; *a leading question* — suggests the answer.

entries.label: noun + noun
entries.meaning: The particular group of people that a product, ad, show or message is designed for.
entries.usage: Common in marketing, media, publishing and presentations: *the target audience for + product*, *reach / appeal to the target audience*. Before planning a talk or an ad, people ask *Who's the target audience?* *Target group* (German *Zielgruppe*) exists too, mostly in research and public health; in marketing and media, Americans usually say *target audience* or *target market*.
entries.pattern: the target audience (for + product) / reach a target audience
examples: The show's **target audience** is kids between six and ten, but plenty of parents watch it too.
Before you design the poster, think about your **target audience**: students or retirees?
The ads clearly missed their **target audience**; teenagers just laughed at them.

drill.sentence: Our {{target audience}} is first-time home buyers, so keep the language simple and skip the jargon.
drill.hint: the people the message is aimed at (noun + noun; the second noun is not *market* or *group*)

entries.related: *target market* — the buyers a company wants; *target demographic* — a group defined by age, income and so on; *niche* — a small, specialized market.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To complete a college or university program successfully and receive the official qualification.
entries.usage: Common in American writing and speech: *earn a degree in + subject*, *earn a degree from + school*, *earn a bachelor's / master's degree*. *Get a degree* is the casual form. British speakers often say *do a degree* for the time when you are studying for one.
entries.pattern: earn a (bachelor's / master's) degree in + subject (from + school)
examples: She **earned a degree** in nursing while working nights at a grocery store.
My grandfather **earned his degree** at sixty-two, the oldest person in his class.
Thousands of adults now **earn a degree** online without quitting their jobs.

drill.sentence: He became the first person in his family to {{earn a degree}}.
drill.hint: successfully finish college with a qualification (verb: not *get*)

mistake.wrong: She made her degree in Berlin.
mistake.right: She earned her degree in Berlin.
mistake.why: English uses *earn* or *get* with *degree*, not *make*; German *einen Abschluss machen* leads learners to *make*.

entries.related: *get a degree* — casual; *graduate (from)* — finish school or college; *drop out* — leave before finishing.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An excellent chance to do or get something, which may not come again.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports commentary and news: *a golden opportunity to + verb*, *miss / waste / pass up a golden opportunity*. It often comes with regret: *We missed a golden opportunity.* Sports commentators use it for a clear chance to score.
entries.pattern: a golden opportunity to + verb / miss / waste a golden opportunity
examples: The striker had **a golden opportunity** to score in the last minute but hit the post.
Three weeks in Japan is **a golden opportunity** for the kids to try new food.
By refusing to negotiate, the company wasted **a golden opportunity** to end the strike.

drill.sentence: My boss is away all week, which gives me {{a golden opportunity}} to clean out my inbox.
drill.hint: an excellent chance that won't come again (adjective: not *perfect* or *great*)

entries.related: *the chance of a lifetime* — a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity; *a window of opportunity* — a short period when something is possible; *pass up* — not take a chance.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Usually; in most cases, though there may be exceptions.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, usually at the start of a sentence: *As a general rule, …*. It introduces advice or a personal habit and leaves room for exceptions. *As a rule* is the shorter form; *generally* and *in general* are simpler alternatives.
entries.pattern: As a general rule, …
examples: **As a general rule**, I don't lend money to friends.
Running shoes, **as a general rule**, last about 300 to 500 miles.
Doctors, **as a general rule**, don't prescribe antibiotics for a cold.

drill.sentence: {{As a general rule}}, the bigger the dog, the shorter its life.
drill.hint: usually, though not always (a four-word phrase)

entries.related: *as a rule* — shorter, same meaning; *a rule of thumb* — a practical, rough guide; *for the most part* — mostly.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make someone respect you through your actions, effort or character over time.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports, leadership and family stories: *earn my respect*, *earn the respect of + group*. *Earn* stresses that respect must be deserved, not demanded. *Gain someone's respect* is similar; *win someone's respect* suggests that you overcame doubt.
entries.pattern: earn someone's respect / earn the respect of + group
examples: The new coach **earned the players' respect** in his first week, when he ran every drill with them.
My stepfather slowly **earned my respect** by always showing up when it mattered.
It took years, but the young surgeon finally **earned the respect** of the older nurses.

drill.sentence: As a young manager, she {{earned their respect}} by listening first and making decisions later.
drill.hint: made them look up to her through her actions (verb: not *gained* or *won*)

entries.related: *gain / win someone's respect* — similar; *command respect* — be naturally respected; *lose someone's respect* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Only a small amount of money, time, staff or materials available for a task.
entries.usage: Common in business, public services, nonprofits and planning: *with limited resources*, *make the most of limited resources*. It is a neutral, slightly formal way to say there isn't enough money or staff. *Scarce resources* is stronger; *on a shoestring* is informal.
entries.pattern: with / on limited resources / make the most of limited resources
examples: The rural school has **limited resources**: one computer lab, no gym and a tiny library.
Nonprofits often do amazing work with very **limited resources**.
Given our **limited resources**, we'll focus on two projects this year instead of five.

drill.sentence: The animal shelter does what it can with {{limited resources}}, but it can't take in every stray.
drill.hint: not much money, staff or supplies (the first word is not *few* or *scarce*)

entries.related: *scarce resources* — very little, formal; *stretched thin* — too much work for the people available; *on a shoestring* — informal, with very little money.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To succeed in entering a place or in getting something, such as information or a service, often after difficulty.
entries.usage: Common in news, security, law and formal writing: *gain access to + building / account / data / healthcare*. It often suggests effort, or that access was not allowed: *Thieves gained access through a window.* In casual talk people say *get into* or *get access to*.
entries.pattern: gain access to + place / information / service
examples: The thieves **gained access to** the house through an unlocked back window.
Someone **gained access to** my email account and sent spam to all my contacts.
The new clinic helps low-income families **gain access to** dental care.

drill.sentence: Firefighters had to break down the door to {{gain access to}} the burning apartment.
drill.hint: get inside (verb + noun + preposition; the verb is not *get*)

mistake.wrong: You can access to the files from home.
mistake.right: You can access the files from home.
mistake.why: The verb *access* takes a direct object; *to* is used only after the noun: *gain access to*.

entries.related: *access* + object — the verb, no *to*; *get into* — informal, enter; *be denied access* — not be allowed in.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Not too expensive for its quality; sold at a fair price.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, ads and recommendations: *reasonably priced food / hotels / wine*. It signals good value, not necessarily cheap, and sounds more positive than *cheap*. American style does not hyphenate *-ly* adverbs, so write *a reasonably priced hotel*.
entries.pattern: reasonably priced + noun / be reasonably priced
examples: The food was great and surprisingly **reasonably priced** for a place in Manhattan.
We're looking for a **reasonably priced** hotel near the beach, nothing fancy.
Their furniture is well made and **reasonably priced**, so it sells out fast.

drill.sentence: For a resort town, the restaurants here are {{reasonably priced}}: dinner for two is under sixty dollars.
drill.hint: fair, not too expensive (adverb + participle; the adverb is not *fairly*)

entries.related: *affordable* — within your budget; *good value* — worth the money; *overpriced* — too expensive.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A small part of a larger group, often one that behaves differently from the rest or does not represent it.
entries.usage: Common in news, statements and discussion, often to defend a group: *only a small minority of fans caused trouble*. It takes *of* + plural noun, and the verb can be singular or plural: *a small minority of fans was / were*. *A tiny minority* is stronger; *the vast majority* is the usual opposite.
entries.pattern: (only) a small minority (of + plural noun)
examples: Most fans were peaceful; only **a small minority** threw bottles after the game.
**A small minority** of customers return almost everything they buy online.
People who work from home every day are still **a small minority** in our town.

drill.sentence: Most dog owners clean up after their pets; it's only {{a small minority}} who leave a mess in the park.
drill.hint: a little part of the group (not *a handful*; the adjective is not *tiny*)

entries.related: *a tiny minority* — even fewer; *a handful* — very few people; *the vast majority* — almost all.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To come to understand something more deeply, often by studying it or experiencing it.
entries.usage: Common in research, education, business and therapy language: *gain (valuable / new) insight into + topic*; *insights* in the plural is also common. The standard preposition is *into*; *insight on* is heard in speech, but *into* is the safe choice in writing.
entries.pattern: gain (valuable / new) insight(s) into + topic
examples: Volunteering at the hospital helped her **gain insight into** what nurses really do.
The customer survey helped the company **gain insight into** why people were canceling.
Reading my grandfather's letters, we **gained insight into** his life during the war.

drill.sentence: Spending a month with a host family let us {{gain insight into}} everyday life in a small Italian town.
drill.hint: come to understand more deeply (verb + noun + preposition; not *learn about*)

mistake.wrong: The trip gave me an insight in Japanese culture.
mistake.right: The trip gave me an insight into Japanese culture.
mistake.why: *Insight* takes *into*; German *Einblick in* leads learners to use *in*.

entries.related: *get a glimpse of* — see a small part; *shed light on* — make something clearer; *understand* — the plain verb.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: At some time in the future that has not been decided yet.
entries.usage: Slightly formal; common in business emails, official notices and announcements: *will take place / be announced / be discussed at a later date*. It is often a polite way to postpone something without a promise. In conversation people say *later* or *some other time*.
entries.pattern: (postponed / discussed / decided) at a later date
examples: The concert has been postponed and will take place **at a later date**.
We can discuss the details **at a later date**; for now, let's just agree on the budget.
You can always add a second bathroom **at a later date** if the family grows.

drill.sentence: The city says the new playground will open {{at a later date}}, but it hasn't given a schedule.
drill.hint: sometime in the future, not yet fixed (a four-word formal phrase)

entries.related: *at some point* — casual; *in due course* — formal, when the right time comes; *to be announced* — not yet decided.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The highest level that something has ever reached.
entries.usage: Very common in news about prices, markets, temperatures and records: *reach / hit / be at an all-time high*. It is used both for worrying things (*rent*) and good news (*attendance*). The opposite is *an all-time low*, which is also used for mood and reputation: *Morale is at an all-time low.*
entries.pattern: reach / hit / be at an all-time high
examples: Home prices in the area hit **an all-time high** last spring.
Attendance at the zoo reached **an all-time high** this summer, thanks to the new baby elephant.
My stress level was at **an all-time high** the week we moved.

drill.sentence: The price of coffee beans is at {{an all-time high}}, so cafés are raising their prices.
drill.hint: the highest level ever (not *record*)

entries.related: *a record high* — the same, common in news; *an all-time low* — the opposite; *peak* — the highest point.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To become liked or used by more and more people over time.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and culture writing: *gain popularity among / with + group*, *quickly / steadily gain popularity*. It describes a gradual process; for a sudden success, *take off* or *go viral* are more common. *Grow in popularity* is a close variant.
entries.pattern: gain popularity (among / with + group)
examples: Pickleball has **gained popularity** with retirees and teenagers alike.
Electric bikes are **gaining popularity** with commuters who don't want to arrive at work sweaty.
The tiny taco stand **gained popularity** through word of mouth.

drill.sentence: Plant-based burgers have {{gained popularity}}, even among people who still eat meat.
drill.hint: become liked by more and more people (not *grown in* or *become popular*)

entries.related: *grow in popularity* — similar; *catch on* — informal, become popular; *lose popularity* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A memory that is very clear and detailed, as if you can still see, hear or feel it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, interviews and memoirs: *have a vivid memory of + noun / -ing*, *one of my most vivid memories*. It can be happy or painful. *Vivid* is about clarity, not emotion; happy memories are *fond memories*.
entries.pattern: have a vivid memory of + noun / -ing
examples: I have **a vivid memory** of my first day of school: the smell of crayons and my mom waving goodbye.
One of my most **vivid memories** is watching fireworks from my grandfather's roof.
People who lived through the earthquake still have **vivid memories** of that morning.

drill.sentence: I still have {{a vivid memory}} of the day our dog got lost in the snow.
drill.hint: a very clear, detailed recollection (adjective: not *clear* or *distinct*)

entries.related: *a clear memory* — plainer; *a hazy / vague memory* — unclear; *fond memories* — happy ones.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make someone believe that they can rely on you, usually over time.
entries.usage: Common in relationships, business, medicine and work with animals: *gain the trust of + group*, *slowly gain someone's trust*. *Earn someone's trust* stresses that it is deserved; *win someone's trust* suggests overcoming doubt. The opposite is *betray* or *lose someone's trust*.
entries.pattern: gain someone's trust / gain the trust of + group
examples: It took weeks to **gain the trust** of the shy rescue dog.
A good salesperson **gains your trust** before trying to sell you anything.
The new police chief has worked hard to **gain the community's trust**.

drill.sentence: It took months for the new babysitter to {{gain our son's trust}}, but now he adores her.
drill.hint: make him feel he could rely on her (verb: not *earn* or *win*)

entries.related: *earn / win someone's trust* — similar; *betray someone's trust* — break it; *trustworthy* — deserving trust.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Taking a very active part in something, often with a lot of time or responsibility.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, biographies and work contexts: *be / get heavily involved in + activity / organization*. It can be positive (community work, a project) or negative (*heavily involved in the scandal*). *Deeply involved* is similar and often more emotional; *actively involved* stresses taking action.
entries.pattern: be / get heavily involved in + noun / -ing
examples: My mom was **heavily involved in** the PTA when we were kids.
He's **heavily involved in** local theater and spends most weekends at rehearsals.
Two of the company's executives were **heavily involved in** the accounting scandal.

drill.sentence: Since retiring, my dad has gotten {{heavily involved in}} the community garden; he's there every morning.
drill.hint: taking a very active part in (adverb: not *deeply* or *really*)

entries.related: *deeply involved* — similar, often emotional; *actively involved* — taking action; *have a hand in* — play a part in.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Happy, warm memories of a past time, place or person.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, speeches and cards: *have fond memories of + place / time / -ing*. It is almost always plural and often used at goodbyes, reunions and memorials. *Fond* adds affection; *good memories* is plainer.
entries.pattern: have (many / such) fond memories of + noun / -ing
examples: I have **fond memories** of summers on my grandparents' farm in Iowa.
At the farewell party, everyone shared **fond memories** of working with Linda.
That old diner holds **fond memories** for a lot of people in this town.

drill.sentence: We spent every Christmas at that cabin, so I have {{fond memories}} of the place.
drill.hint: affectionate recollections (adjective: not *good*, *happy*, *warm* or *great*)

entries.related: *happy memories* — plainer; *bittersweet memories* — happy and sad at once; *a vivid memory* — very clear, not necessarily happy.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To say or show that you want to know more about something or to take part in it.
entries.usage: Common in business, hiring, real estate and formal emails: *express (strong) interest in + noun / -ing*. It signals interest without any commitment. In conversation people usually say *I'd be interested in* or *I'm interested in*.
entries.pattern: express (an / strong) interest in + noun / -ing
examples: Several buyers have **expressed interest in** the house, so we might get offers this week.
Three students **expressed interest in** starting a chess club, so the school agreed to try it.
Thank you for **expressing interest in** the position; we'll contact you next week.

drill.sentence: Two other teams have {{expressed interest in}} signing the young pitcher.
drill.hint: said they'd like to (verb: not *shown*)

mistake.wrong: She expressed her interest for the job.
mistake.right: She expressed her interest in the job.
mistake.why: *Interest* takes *in*; German *Interesse für* leads learners to use *for*.

entries.related: *show interest in* — similar, through behavior; *take an interest in* — start to care about; *lose interest in* — stop caring.

entries.term: in the early stages of something
entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Near the beginning of a process, project, illness or relationship.
entries.usage: Common in news, medicine, business and conversation: *in the early stages of + noun*, *still in the early stages*. It often warns that results are not known yet: *It's still in the early stages.* The opposite is *in the final* or *late stages*.
entries.pattern: in the early stages of + noun / still in the early stages
examples: The cancer was caught **in the early stages**, so her chances are very good.
We're **in the early stages of** planning the wedding, so nothing is booked yet.
The investigation is still **in the early stages**, police said.

drill.sentence: Work on the new library is only {{in the early stages}}, so it won't open for at least two years.
drill.hint: near the beginning (the adjective is not *first*)

entries.related: *early on* — near the start; *in its infancy* — very new, still developing; *in the final stages* — near the end.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Buses, trains, subways and other shared ways of traveling that anyone can use for a fare.
entries.usage: The American term; British English says *public transport*. Typical forms are *take / use public transportation* and *get somewhere by public transportation*. Americans also say *public transit* or just *transit*, especially in city planning and news.
entries.pattern: take / use public transportation / by public transportation
examples: In New York, most people use **public transportation** instead of owning a car.
Is it easy to get to the stadium by **public transportation**?
The city plans to spend more on **public transportation** to cut traffic downtown.

drill.sentence: We didn't rent a car in Chicago; we got around on {{public transportation}} the whole week.
drill.hint: buses and trains anyone can use (the second word is not *transit*)

mistake.wrong: There is a good public transportation in this city.
mistake.right: There is good public transportation in this city.
mistake.why: *Public transportation* is uncountable, so it takes no *a*.

entries.related: *public transport* — British; *public transit / transit* — American, common in planning; *commute* — a regular trip to work.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To ask an expert or an experienced person for help or an opinion before you decide something.
entries.usage: Formal; common in official guidance, legal and medical texts and the news: *seek advice from + person*, *seek advice on + topic*, *seek legal / medical / professional advice*. In conversation people say *ask for advice* or *get advice*.
entries.pattern: seek (legal / medical) advice (from + someone / on + topic)
examples: If the pain lasts more than a week, **seek advice** from your doctor.
Before signing anything, she **sought legal advice**.
Many first-time buyers **seek advice** on mortgages from relatives who've been through it.

drill.sentence: If you're unsure about your rights as a tenant, {{seek advice}} from a housing counselor.
drill.hint: ask for expert guidance (formal verb + noun; not *get* or *ask for*)

mistake.wrong: I need to seek an advice from a lawyer.
mistake.right: I need to seek advice from a lawyer.
mistake.why: *Advice* is uncountable, so it never takes *a* or *an*; say *advice* or *a piece of advice*.

entries.related: *ask for advice* — the everyday form; *consult* — formal, ask an expert; *take someone's advice* — follow it.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Liked and praised by the people who see, read, hear or use something.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, reports and work updates: *be well received by + audience / critics*. It is often used modestly about your own work: *My talk was well received.* Before a noun it takes a hyphen (*a well-received book*), but not after a verb.
entries.pattern: be well received (by + audience) / a well-received + noun
examples: Her first novel was **well received** by critics, and now it's being made into a movie.
My lasagna was surprisingly **well received** at the potluck, considering I burned the top.
The new bus schedule has been **well received** by commuters.

drill.sentence: The new skate park has been {{well received}}: it's packed with kids every afternoon.
drill.hint: liked and praised (adverb + participle; the participle is not *liked*)

entries.related: *a hit* — informal, very popular; *poorly received* — the opposite; *critically acclaimed* — praised by critics.

entries.label: verb + object + adjective
entries.meaning: To consider someone to be the person who must take the blame for something or deal with its results.
entries.usage: Common in news, law, workplaces and family arguments: *hold someone (personally) responsible for + noun / -ing*. It is a serious way to assign blame and often works as a warning: *I'll hold you responsible if …* *Hold someone accountable* is close and stresses that they must explain or face consequences.
entries.pattern: hold someone (personally) responsible for + noun / -ing
examples: If anything happens to my car while you're borrowing it, I'll **hold you responsible**.
Parents can be **held responsible** for damage their children cause to other people's property.
Angry investors **held the CEO responsible** for the company's collapse.

drill.sentence: The airline says it cannot {{be held responsible}} for items left on the plane.
drill.hint: be blamed or made to pay (the adjective is not *liable* or *accountable*)

mistake.wrong: The neighbors made me responsible for the broken window.
mistake.right: The neighbors held me responsible for the broken window.
mistake.why: *Make someone responsible for* means to put them in charge of something; to blame someone, say *hold someone responsible* (German *verantwortlich machen*).

entries.related: *hold someone accountable* — make them answer for it; *blame someone for* — plainer; *take responsibility for* — accept the blame yourself.

entries.term: be in a position to do something
entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To be able to do something because of your situation, knowledge, money or authority.
entries.usage: Common in formal speech, business emails and news, often in the negative as a polite refusal: *I'm not in a position to comment.* It sounds more formal and less personal than *can* or *be able to*. *Be in no position to* is different: it means you have no right to do something (*You're in no position to judge*).
entries.pattern: be (not) in a position to + verb
examples: I'm afraid I'm **not in a position to** discuss the details of the case.
Once we've paid off the car, we'll **be in a position to** save for a house.
With two games left, the team is **in a position to** win the division.

drill.sentence: We'd love to help, but right now we're not {{in a position to}} lend anyone money.
drill.hint: able, given our situation (four words; not just *able to*)

entries.related: *be able to* — plainer; *be in no position to* — have no right to, often critical; *be well placed to* — have a good chance to.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To officially tell people about a danger or a possible problem, usually as an authority or organization.
entries.usage: Common in news, weather reports, health and safety: *issue a warning about / against + noun*, *issue a warning to + people*, *issue a warning that …*. The subject is usually official: the weather service, the police, a company, a health department. For a personal warning, people say *warn someone* or *give someone a warning*.
entries.pattern: issue a warning (about / against + noun / to + people / that …)
examples: The National Weather Service has **issued a warning** for heavy snow tonight.
Police **issued a warning** about fake parking tickets left on cars downtown.
Has the city **issued a warning** about the heat yet, or are they waiting until tomorrow?

drill.sentence: The health department {{issued a warning}} against eating oysters from the bay after the storm.
drill.hint: officially told the public about the danger (verb: not *put out*, *sent out* or *gave*)

entries.related: *warn* — the plain verb; *give someone a warning* — often personal; *sound the alarm* — call attention to a danger.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Proven and recorded in many sources, so that there is plenty of evidence for it.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, science, law and serious discussion: *It's well documented that …*, *the well-documented risks of + noun*. It claims there is a lot of evidence, so it is stronger than *well known*. Hyphenate it before a noun (*a well-documented problem*), but not after a verb.
entries.pattern: it's well documented that … / be well documented / a well-documented + noun
examples: The health risks of smoking are **well documented**.
His temper was **well documented**; he'd been thrown out of three games that season.
It's **well documented** that kids who read for fun do better in school.

drill.sentence: The bridge's problems were {{well documented}}: inspectors had reported cracks for years.
drill.hint: recorded in many reports, with lots of proof (the participle is not *known*)

entries.related: *well known* — many people know it, with or without evidence; *well established* — accepted for a long time; *anecdotal* — based on stories, not proof.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To create a difficulty that someone must deal with.
entries.usage: Common in news, business, academic writing and formal speech: *pose a (real / serious) challenge to / for + someone*. The subject is the problem, not a person: *The heat poses a challenge for runners.* The same verb goes with *threat*, *risk* and *problem*.
entries.pattern: pose a (real / serious) challenge to / for + someone
examples: The steep hills **pose a real challenge** for cyclists on the last day of the race.
Rising rents **pose a challenge** to young families who want to stay in the city.
Old buildings without elevators **pose a challenge** for wheelchair users.

drill.sentence: Snow and narrow mountain roads {{pose a challenge}} for delivery drivers every winter.
drill.hint: create a difficulty (verb: not *present*; the noun is not *problem*)

entries.related: *present a challenge* — the same, slightly more formal; *pose a threat / risk* — same verb; *rise to the challenge* — deal with it successfully.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Hopes or demands that cannot reasonably be met in a given situation.
entries.usage: Common in relationships, parenting, work and self-help: *have / set / create unrealistic expectations*, followed by *of / for + person* or *about + thing*. It is usually critical. *High expectations* can be positive; *unrealistic* means too high to be fair.
entries.pattern: have / set / create unrealistic expectations (of / for + someone / about + noun)
examples: Social media can give teenagers **unrealistic expectations** about how their bodies should look.
My first boss had **unrealistic expectations**; he wanted a week's work done in a single day.
Don't set **unrealistic expectations** for your first marathon; just aim to finish.

drill.sentence: Wedding shows on TV give couples {{unrealistic expectations}} about what they can afford.
drill.hint: hopes that can't reasonably be met (adjective: not *false* or *high*)

entries.related: *high expectations* — ambitious, not necessarily unfair; *a reality check* — a reminder of the facts; *set the bar too high* — expect too much.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To succeed in dealing with something that blocks your progress.
entries.usage: Common in personal stories, speeches, sports, business and self-help: *overcome obstacles / challenges / difficulties*. It is often plural and about personal effort: *She overcame huge obstacles to get where she is.* *Get past* is the informal alternative, and *clear a hurdle* is similar.
entries.pattern: overcome an / many obstacle(s) (to + verb)
examples: Growing up deaf, she **overcame many obstacles** to become a lawyer.
To open the café, we had to **overcome an obstacle** we hadn't expected: the city's parking rules.
The team **overcame every obstacle** this season, including injuries to three starters.

drill.sentence: With help from a tutor, my son finally {{overcame his biggest obstacle}}: fear of math tests.
drill.hint: dealt successfully with the thing that held him back most (verb: not *got past* or *conquered*; the noun is not *challenge*)

entries.related: *overcome a challenge / difficulty* — similar; *get past* — informal; *a stumbling block* — a problem that stops progress.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The unpleasant truth of a situation, which people may not want to accept.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, speeches and serious conversation: *the harsh reality is that …*, *the harsh reality of + noun*, *face the harsh reality*. It sounds frank and slightly dramatic. *The hard truth* and *the cold reality* are similar.
entries.pattern: the harsh reality is (that) … / the harsh reality of + noun
examples: **The harsh reality** is that many new restaurants close within a few years.
In Los Angeles, she quickly faced **the harsh reality** of the acting business: hundreds of auditions and very few roles.
Nobody warned us about **the harsh reality** of life with twins: almost no sleep for a year.

drill.sentence: We'd love a bigger house, but {{the harsh reality}} is that we can't afford one in this neighborhood.
drill.hint: the unpleasant truth (adjective: not *sad* or *cold*; the noun is not *truth*)

entries.related: *the hard truth* — similar; *face facts* — accept reality; *a rude awakening* — a sudden, unpleasant realization.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Also true, but less so than the thing mentioned before.
entries.usage: Common in writing, reports and careful speech, usually after the main item: *A affects X and, to a lesser extent, Y.* It is often set off by commas. *To a lesser degree* means the same; the opposite is *to a greater extent*.
entries.pattern: A and, to a lesser extent, B
examples: The storm damaged homes in Miami and, **to a lesser extent**, Fort Lauderdale.
My knee hurts most when I run and, **to a lesser extent**, when I climb stairs.
Rents have jumped in the city center. **To a lesser extent**, the same is true of the suburbs.

drill.sentence: My kids love soccer and, {{to a lesser extent}}, basketball.
drill.hint: also, but not as much (the noun is not *degree*)

mistake.wrong: Prices rose in the city and, in a lesser extent, in the suburbs.
mistake.right: Prices rose in the city and, to a lesser extent, in the suburbs.
mistake.why: The phrase uses *to*, like *to some extent* and *to a great extent*; German *in geringerem Maße* leads learners to use *in*.

entries.related: *to a lesser degree* — the same; *to some extent* — partly; *to a greater extent* — more so.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A strong, active interest in something, so that you want to learn about it or take part in it.
entries.usage: Common in cover letters, biographies, job ads and polite conversation: *have / show / take a keen interest in + noun*. *Take a keen interest in* often means paying close attention to someone or something: *She takes a keen interest in her students.* *Be keen on* (*like*) sounds British, but *a keen interest* is normal in American English too.
entries.pattern: have / show / take a keen interest in + noun / -ing
examples: From an early age, he showed **a keen interest in** how machines work.
My neighbor takes **a keen interest in** everyone's business, which gets a little annoying.
Applicants should have **a keen interest in** local history and enjoy talking to visitors.

drill.sentence: She's always had {{a keen interest in}} birds and can name almost any species by its song.
drill.hint: a strong, active fascination with (adjective: not *strong*, *deep* or *real*)

entries.related: *a passing interest* — weak and brief; *be passionate about* — stronger, emotional; *be keen on* — like something, mostly British.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Earning a good salary, or, about a job, paying a good salary.
entries.usage: Used for people and jobs: *a well-paid job*, *nurses here are well paid*. Hyphenate it before a noun, not after a verb. The opposite is *poorly paid* or *underpaid*; *highly paid* is stronger and often used for executives and top professionals.
entries.pattern: be well paid / a well-paid + job / person
examples: The job is **well paid**, but the hours are terrible.
Plumbers around here are surprisingly **well paid**, so my nephew is thinking of becoming one.
She left a **well-paid** position at a bank to teach high school math.

drill.sentence: Truck drivers on long routes are fairly {{well paid}}, but they spend weeks away from home.
drill.hint: earning good money (not *highly*; the participle is not *compensated*)

entries.related: *highly paid* — very well paid; *underpaid* — paid less than deserved; *lucrative* — about a job or business that makes a lot of money.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To do something illegal that can be punished by law.
entries.usage: The standard verb with *crime* is *commit*, which also goes with *murder*, *fraud* and *an offense*. It is neutral and common in news, law and conversation: *He was accused of a crime he didn't commit.* *Break the law* is the everyday alternative.
entries.pattern: commit a (serious / violent) crime
examples: Police believe the same man **committed both crimes**, since the break-ins were almost identical.
Taking a few apples from a neighbor's tree isn't exactly **committing a crime**.
Anyone who **commits a crime** while on parole can be sent straight back to prison.

drill.sentence: He had never {{committed a crime}} in his life, so the arrest came as a total shock.
drill.hint: done anything illegal (not *broken the law*)

mistake.wrong: He did a crime when he was young.
mistake.right: He committed a crime when he was young.
mistake.why: In standard English *crime* takes *commit*; *do a crime* sounds non-native outside fixed sayings like *If you do the crime, you do the time*.

entries.related: *break the law* — everyday form, also for small offenses; *commit an offense* — formal; *a petty crime* — a small one, like shoplifting.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A clear, honest and direct answer that does not avoid the question.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism, usually in complaints or demands: *get / give a straight answer*, *I just want a straight answer.* It is often negative: *I can't get a straight answer out of anyone.* *A direct answer* is similar but less emotional.
entries.pattern: give / get a straight answer (out of + someone)
examples: I asked the mechanic three times what was wrong, but I couldn't get **a straight answer**.
Just give me **a straight answer**: are you coming to the wedding or not?
Reporters pushed the team's owner for **a straight answer** about the stadium deal.

drill.sentence: I can never get {{a straight answer}} out of my teenage son about where he's going on Friday nights.
drill.hint: a clear, honest reply (adjective: not *direct*, *clear* or *real*)

entries.related: *a direct answer* — similar, less emotional; *beat around the bush* — avoid saying something directly; *dodge the question* — avoid answering.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To officially approve a new law, usually by a vote of a legislature or council.
entries.usage: Common in news and civics: *pass a law banning / requiring + noun*, *pass a law that …*. The subject is a lawmaking body (Congress, a state legislature, a city council), not a single person. In the US, a bill is *passed* by lawmakers and then *signed into law* by the governor or president.
entries.pattern: pass a law banning / requiring + noun / pass a law that …
examples: The city council **passed a law** requiring dog owners to keep their pets on a leash in parks.
The state **passed a law** last year that bans cellphones during class.
If enough people complain, maybe they'll **pass a law** about leaf blowers.

drill.sentence: After several accidents, the town {{passed a law}} limiting e-scooters to fifteen miles per hour.
drill.hint: officially approved new legislation (verb: not *approved* or *adopted*)

entries.related: *enact a law* — formal; *repeal a law* — cancel it; *a bill* — a proposed law before it is passed.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Costing more than the amount of money that was planned.
entries.usage: Common in business, construction, government and home projects: *go / run / come in over budget*, often with *behind schedule*. It can take an amount in front: *two million dollars over budget*. The opposite is *under budget*; *on budget* means exactly as planned.
entries.pattern: go / run / come in (amount) over budget (and behind schedule)
examples: Our kitchen remodel went **over budget** by almost ten thousand dollars.
The new stadium opened two years late and 300 million dollars **over budget**.
We're already **over budget** for groceries this month, so no takeout this weekend.

drill.sentence: The costumes for the school play cost more than expected, so the drama club is now {{over budget}}.
drill.hint: spending more than planned (not *in the red*)

entries.related: *under budget* — costing less than planned; *behind schedule* — late; *in the red* — losing money or in debt.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something that is completely different from another thing in every important way.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing to stress a contrast: *the exact opposite of + noun*, *do the exact opposite*, *Actually, it's the exact opposite.* It often corrects someone or describes a surprising result. *The complete opposite* and *the polar opposite* are similar; *quite the opposite* is more formal.
entries.pattern: the exact opposite (of + noun) / do the exact opposite
examples: My brother is loud and messy; I'm **the exact opposite**.
I told the kids to stay inside, and of course they did **the exact opposite**.
The diet was supposed to give me more energy, but it had **the exact opposite** effect.

drill.sentence: People think my sister is shy, but at parties she's {{the exact opposite}}: she's always the first one dancing.
drill.hint: completely different in every way (adjective: not *complete*, *total* or *polar*)

entries.related: *the complete / polar opposite* — similar; *quite the opposite* — formal, used as a correction; *the reverse* — the opposite order or direction.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Badly hurt in an accident or attack, with injuries that may be dangerous or need hospital care.
entries.usage: Common in news reports and official statements: *be seriously injured in + accident*. It is stronger than *slightly injured* and weaker than *critically injured*, which means the person's life is in danger. *Badly hurt* is the everyday equivalent.
entries.pattern: be seriously injured (in + accident / attack)
examples: Two people were **seriously injured** when a truck crashed into a bus stop.
He was **seriously injured** in a skiing accident and spent months learning to walk again.
Luckily, no one was **seriously injured**, though several fans needed stitches.

drill.sentence: A cyclist was {{seriously injured}} when the door of a parked car suddenly opened in front of her.
drill.hint: hurt in a dangerous way (adverb + participle; the adverb is not *badly*, *severely* or *critically*)

entries.related: *critically injured* — life in danger; *minor injuries* — not serious; *badly hurt* — everyday equivalent.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The final option, used only when everything else has failed.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *as a last resort*, *only as a last resort*, *be a last resort*. It suggests the option is unpleasant, risky or expensive. *Resort* here means an option you turn to, not a vacation resort.
entries.pattern: as a last resort / only as a last resort / be a last resort
examples: Driving around the block at midnight was our **last resort** to get the baby to sleep.
Many doctors say surgery should be **a last resort** for back pain.
**As a last resort**, I called my landlord's mother, and the heat was fixed the next day.

drill.sentence: I only use my credit card as {{a last resort}}, when I have no cash left at all.
drill.hint: the final option when nothing else works (not *backup* or *fallback*)

entries.related: *a fallback* — a backup plan; *Plan B* — informal, a second option; *in desperation* — because nothing else is left.
